title: In mouse V1, EM synapse number per connection predicted slice PSP amplitude across inhibitory cell-class pairs, but release probability, not synapse number, set trial-to-trial reliability
abstract: Question: does the number of synapses per connection predict the strength and the trial-to-trial reliability of cortical connections? We linked two Allen Institute datasets from mouse V1 at the level of cell-class pairs. MICrONS EM (v1507; 1,619 proofread axons, 242,139 connections) gave distance-matched synapses per connection. Allen Synaptic Physiology r2.1 (1,564 slice connections, 750 experiments) gave PSP amplitude, noise-corrected 1/CV^2 of first pulses, and release-model probability p. We used 28 class pairs with Pvalb, Sst and Vip interneurons and five excitatory classes. The pre-registered primary test passed: EM synapse number correlated with reliability (Spearman rho 0.62, 95% bootstrap interval 0.38 to 0.76, n = 24). But the correlation came from the difference between excitatory and inhibitory sources. Within source sign it was absent (stratified rho 0.03, p = 0.44). Release probability explained most of the reliability (R^2 0.63); synapse number added an uncertain term (0.71 +/- 0.65). Within inhibitory sources, synapse number predicted amplitude (rho 0.74, n = 19; log-log slope 1.40 +/- 0.36), and conductance and input-resistance controls agreed. Within excitatory sources, the link was not clear (rho 0.07, n = 9), and the range was narrow. With log p and source sign in the model, log amplitude scaled with log synapse number with slope 1.03 +/- 0.39 (post hoc). Thus synapse counts predict mean strength, mainly for inhibition, but target-specific release probability sets most class differences in reliability. Limitations: one EM mouse against many slice mice, class-level comparison only, slice truncation, low single-trial SNR, dependent class pairs, and post-hoc controls.
